front_blocks.md: What is a covalent bond?

back_blocks.md: A covalent bond is the **electrostatic attraction** between a **shared pair of electrons** and the nuclei of the two bonded atoms. Both atoms contribute one electron to the shared pair, giving each atom a full outer shell.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Covalent bonds form between metal and non-metal atoms.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Covalent bonds form between **non-metal atoms only**. When a metal reacts with a non-metal, ionic bonds form instead.

front_blocks.md: A covalent bond forms when a **..........** of electrons is **..........** between two atoms. The bond arises from the electrostatic attraction between these electrons and the **..........** of both atoms.

back_blocks.md: A covalent bond forms when a **pair** of electrons is **shared** between two atoms. The bond arises from the electrostatic attraction between these electrons and the **nuclei** of both atoms.

front_blocks.md: Why do two chlorine atoms form a covalent bond with each other?

back_blocks.md: Each chlorine atom has 7 electrons in its outer shell and needs one more to achieve a **full outer shell** of 8. By **sharing one pair of electrons**, both chlorine atoms gain a full outer shell, forming a stable Cl<sub>2</sub> molecule.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
In a dot-and-cross diagram of a covalent molecule, the shared electrons are shown in the overlapping region between the two atoms.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
The **overlapping region** represents the **shared electron pair**. Electrons from one atom are shown as dots and from the other as crosses, so the origin of each electron is clear.

back_blocks.md: Water (H<sub>2</sub>O) contains two **covalent** bonds, with each hydrogen atom sharing a pair of electrons with the **oxygen** atom to give each atom a full outer **shell**.

front_blocks.md: Give two differences between ionic and covalent bonding.

back_blocks.md: In ionic bonding, electrons are **transferred** from a metal to a non-metal to form oppositely charged ions.
In covalent bonding, electrons are **shared** between non-metal atoms, forming molecules with no overall charge.

In covalent bonding, electrons are **shared** between non-metal atoms, forming molecules with no overall charge.

front_blocks.md: What is a double covalent bond?

back_blocks.md: A double covalent bond forms when two atoms **share two pairs of electrons**. This occurs when each atom needs to share more than one pair of electrons to achieve a **full outer shell**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Nitrogen (N<sub>2</sub>) contains a triple bond because each nitrogen atom needs three more electrons to fill its outer shell.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
Each nitrogen atom has 5 electrons in its outer shell and needs 3 more to fill it. By sharing **3 pairs of electrons**, both nitrogen atoms achieve a full outer shell, forming a **triple bond**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
In ethene (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>), the two carbon atoms are joined by a double bond.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
In ethene, each carbon atom shares **two pairs of electrons** with the other carbon, forming a **double bond**. This allows both carbon atoms to achieve a full outer shell.

front_blocks.md: Why must oxygen (O<sub>2</sub>) form a double bond rather than a single bond?

back_blocks.md: Each oxygen atom has 6 electrons in its outer shell and needs **2 more** to achieve a full outer shell of 8. A single bond would only provide 1 extra electron per atom. By sharing **2 pairs of electrons** (a double bond), both oxygen atoms gain a full outer shell.

front_blocks.md: What are the melting and boiling points of simple molecular compounds, and why?

back_blocks.md: Simple molecular compounds have **low melting and boiling points** because only **weak intermolecular forces** need to be overcome to separate the molecules. The covalent bonds within each molecule remain intact during melting or boiling.

cards.front_md: What are the melting and boiling points of simple molecular compounds, and why?

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Simple molecular compounds have low melting points because their covalent bonds are weak.

back_blocks.md: **False.**

The covalent bonds within molecules are strong. Simple molecular compounds have low melting points because the **intermolecular forces** between molecules are **weak** and require little energy to overcome.

front_blocks.md: Simple molecular compounds are usually **..........** or **..........** at room temperature because the **..........** forces between molecules require little energy to overcome.

back_blocks.md: Simple molecular compounds are usually **liquids** or **gases** at room temperature because the **intermolecular** forces between molecules require little energy to overcome.

front_blocks.md: Why do simple molecular compounds not conduct electricity?

back_blocks.md: Simple molecular compounds have **no free electrons or ions**. All electrons are held in covalent bonds within the molecules and cannot move freely to carry a charge, making these substances **electrical insulators**.

cards.front_md: Why do simple molecular compounds not conduct electricity?

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Larger simple molecules tend to have higher melting points than smaller ones.

back_blocks.md: **True.**

As molecule size increases, there are more electrons available to create **stronger intermolecular forces** between molecules. More energy is needed to overcome these forces, so larger molecules have higher melting and boiling points.

front_blocks.md: Why is methane (CH<sub>4</sub>) a gas at room temperature while larger alkanes such as decane are liquids?

back_blocks.md: Methane is a small molecule with **weak intermolecular forces** between molecules, so little energy is needed to separate them and it exists as a gas at room temperature.
Decane is a much larger molecule with **stronger intermolecular forces**, requiring more energy to overcome, so it is a liquid.
